Therefore, the attribution to Fennick Yost is considered very reliable by current historical standards.

Three separate, contemporaneous primary sources support this: (1) her 1842 diary entry in which she expressly says she “coined” the line, (2) an 1845 brass plaque on a loom, signed by her, repeating that claim, and (3) the 1848 minutes of the Guild of Weavers recording the proverb and noting Fael as its originator.  Because these documents are independent, date from within a six-year span, and no rival claimant is known, the attribution to Olyndra Fael is considered very well established by primary historical evidence.

The maximum depth of Lake Muroq is reported as 814 meters. This figure is well established: it originates from the 2018 multi-beam sonar survey (P1), is adopted in the Ministry of Water’s official registry (P2), and was independently confirmed by a crewed submersible descent (P3). Subsequent journal and textbook references (P4, P5) all cite the same value. Because multiple, mutually independent primary measurements converge on 814 m and it is the official benchmark for state records, the measurement is considered highly reliable with strong supporting evidence.

All available primary measurements converge on a top sprinting velocity of about 83 km/h for an adult Glandic Fex.  

Evidence base
• P3: Official Species Performance Registry entry, certified by the International Wildlife Biometrics Board using standardized track testing in a controlled setting (instrumented course, no citation needed).  
• P1: 2021 peer-reviewed field study employing GPS collars and radar traps; peak 83 km/h recorded in 14 adults across six months.  
• P2: 1998 expedition vehicle-pacing log; anecdotal but instrument-assisted, also reports 83 km/h.  
Secondary summaries (P4, P5) repeat these primary findings.

Reliability assessment
Two independent, instrument-based primary studies (P3 laboratory track test; P1 long-term field telemetry) both report the same value and use modern, quantitative methods. Even though sample sizes are modest (one standardized test in P3, 14 individuals in P1), the concordance between controlled-environment and natural-environment measurements makes the 83 km/h figure well supported. The older vehicle-pacing observation (P2) provides historical corroboration but is of lower methodological rigor.

Conclusion
Maximum running speed ≈ 83 km/h; evidence strength: high—multiple, independent, instrumented studies with consistent results, though additional large-sample studies would further solidify the figure.

All three primary pieces of evidence now cited (a royal charter, a monastic ledger entry, and an archaeological residue report) give the same date: 1147.

• Royal charter (Charter of King Otho II) – a contemporaneous document that explicitly mentions the exemption of “the newly invented Bregnari flatbread” and supplies the year 1147. If the parchment and seal are genuine, this is strong written evidence, but the charter has not been subjected to modern diplomatic or palaeographic authentication in the literature provided.

• Monastic ledger (Abbey of St. Bregnar, Folio 42v) – likewise purports to be a contemporary record dated to Michaelmas 1147. Medieval monastic accounts can be reliable day-to-day records, yet we have only a single folio cited, with no external corroboration that the folio itself was written in 1147 rather than copied later.

• Archaeological residue (Sample BRG-09) – radiocarbon methods can usually narrow dates to a range of a few decades, not to a precise calendar year. The claim that AMS dating “pinpoints the exact origin … first baked in 1147” almost certainly overstates the method’s resolution. At best, it supports a mid-12th-century horizon.

Overall reliability: The convergence of two putative contemporaneous written sources on the same year provides moderate support that the recipe originated circa 1147. However, the lack of modern scholarly verification of the documents and the over-precise use of radiocarbon dating mean the exact year should be treated cautiously. The best-supported conclusion is that Bregnari flatbread emerged in the mid-12th century, probably around 1147, but the evidence for that specific year is not firmly established.

The Treaty of Paldor was signed in 1394. This date is very firmly established: the original treaty parchment in the national archives (primary legal document) is explicitly dated 1394, an eyewitness diary from Brother Thomas written at the time records the same year, and independent dendrochronological analysis of the signing table yields a felling date that also points to 1394. Modern historical studies and encyclopedias cite these converging primary and scientific sources. Because multiple independent, contemporaneous, and physical lines of evidence agree, historians regard the 1394 signing date as highly secure and well-supported.

The central tower of the Qalari Citadel is 142 metres tall. This figure is very well-established: it appears in two independent 14th-century primary documents (stonemason charters and the Master Builder’s Log) and is confirmed by a 2023 high-resolution Lidar/photogrammetry survey. Thus historical records and modern instrumentation converge on the same measurement, giving it strong evidential support.

Current consensus lists 19 natural satellites (all classified as minor moons) orbiting the rogue planet Hylosia. This number is regarded as highly reliable: it appears in the International Astronomical Union’s official registry, is confirmed by independent ground-based observations (Keck Observatory logs), and matches in-situ detections from a Deep Space Network probe fly-by. Because multiple independent primary sources converge on the same count and no contradictory measurements are reported, the figure is considered well-established within the astronomical community.

The traditional penalty for a Kaelen strike in Tesh-kora is the deduction of three stones from the offending player’s score.  This rule is strongly attested: it appears in the 14th-century Vellum of Rules (P1), is corroborated by a 17th-century scoring abacus whose foul-lever automatically removes exactly three stones (P2; confirmed in P5), and is described in an 1822 referee’s journal (P3). Later scholarly syntheses (P4, P5) echo these primary sources.  Because multiple independent primary sources—textual, mechanical, and eyewitness—agree, historians consider the “three-stone deduction” rule to be well-documented and highly reliable.

Elias Thorne—the scientist who discovered the Lymric Constant—was originally a self-taught clockmaker.  This claim is strongly supported: three independent, contemporaneous primary sources (the 1742 Guild Registry entry, the engraved 1745 chronometer, and Lord Cavendish’s 1746 letter) all state or physically attest to his occupation, and later secondary works merely echo these records.  No contradictory documentation has surfaced, so the biographical detail is considered well-established.

The highest officially recorded air temperature in the Nethari Highlands is 54.2 °C, measured by automated weather Station 44-B at 14:00 local time (date not specified in the retrieved sources).

Reliability assessment
• Instrument quality: According to the Station 44-B log (P1), the reading came from redundant platinum-resistance thermometers whose calibration had been verified, which is a high-accuracy, standard meteorological setup.
• Independent checks: The same 54.2 °C value appears in three separate lines of evidence—(1) the raw station log (P1), (2) the national Ministry of Climatology’s certified extremes database (P2), and (3) a peer-reviewed synthesis of automated-station data (P4).  A field observer’s diary (P3) also reported the identical value with a manual mercury thermometer, offering an additional—but less rigorous—corroboration.
• Institutional validation: The Ministry’s decadal climate review board formally certified the record (P2), and the weather-science journal article (P4) states that the measurement passed quality-control checks.

Limitations: All sources ultimately trace back to a single site and a single thermal event; there is no second station in the Highlands that captured the same spike, so spatial replication is lacking.  Nonetheless, the redundant sensors, documented calibration, and governmental & peer-review certification provide strong support.

Overall, the evidence for the 54.2 °C record is considered high-confidence by current climatological standards, though future data from additional stations could still revise the absolute extreme.

The crimson hexagon on the seal of the Maruvian Senate symbolizes the six founding families of the republic. This explanation is very well established: it is codified in the original Senate decree (P1), confirmed in the contemporary engraver’s journal (P2), corroborated by the inscription on the surviving stamping matrix (P3), and repeated in secondary scholarly and reference works (P4, P5). Together, these independent primary documents and their scholarly citations provide strong, virtually uncontested evidence for the interpretation.

The Rhapsody of Kinthar is attributed to the late-19th-century composer Jorlan Fane.  Multiple independent, primary-level sources all point to Fane, making the attribution exceptionally secure: (1) an official 1892 Royal Commission payment record lists Fane as the recipient for the score (P2, echoed in P5); (2) a contemporary eyewitness letter describes Fane coaching musicians with the new work in rehearsal (P1, cited in P4); and (3) modern forensic analysis of a surviving autograph manuscript shows a 99.8 % handwriting/ink match with known Fane samples (P3).  Because these lines of evidence are direct, mutually consistent, and come from both period documents and modern scientific study, historians regard the attribution as virtually certain.

The defining or “signature” ingredient of authentic Osken broth is powdered lumis root.  This claim is strongly supported: it appears in Chef Maro’s original 1815 recipe diaries (primary historical source), is codified in the legally binding 1842 Osken Culinary Charter, and is empirically confirmed by modern laboratory analyses (GC-MS) of 50 heritage broth samples that all contained lumis-root–specific alkaloids.  Multiple independent lines of evidence—historical, legal, and chemical—converge, so the tradition is considered well-established and robustly documented.

The record winning margin in the Crystalline Regatta of Ysmera is eighty-two (82) seconds.

Documentation strength: High. Two independent primary sources—the Official Timekeeper Log (P1) and the Ysmera Observatory’s calibrated optical sensor data (P2)—each record the same 82-second margin. Secondary analyses (P4, P5) and a contemporaneous personal diary (P3) corroborate these figures. Because the two primary sources are instrument-based or formally certified and concur to the second, historians consider the 82-second record to be firmly established with minimal uncertainty.

All available evidence points to 1738 as the founding year of the frontier town of Kestria. The date is exceptionally well documented: (1) an official Royal Charter explicitly states the town was incorporated in 1738; (2) a contemporary pioneer diary records the establishment that same spring; and (3) dendrochronological analysis of the timbers in Kestria’s first structure dates the wood to late 1737, matching construction in early 1738. These three independent, primary-source lines of evidence—legal, eyewitness, and scientific—are further echoed by later secondary works. Consequently, historians regard 1738 as the town’s founding year with very high confidence.

The refractive index of Jastril alloy is 2.84. This value is supported by multiple converging sources—direct ellipsometry measurements (P1), an ISO-validated materials certificate (P2), and an independent lab record (P3)—and is echoed in secondary reviews (P4, P5). Because the primary data are consistent and one source is an internationally certified standard, the measurement can be considered well established with moderate-to-high confidence, though large-scale independent replications are still limited.

All available primary sources agree that Cydron was born in the coastal city of Bexil. The evidence is unusually strong for an ancient figure: (1) an official civic birth ledger bearing the magistrate’s seal (P1), (2) a contemporaneous inscribed stele excavated from his family estate and scientifically dated to his lifetime (P2), and (3) a firsthand letter from his contemporary General Varo describing a visit to Cydron’s childhood home in Bexil (P3). Because these three independent, datable, and mutually corroborating sources point to the same location—and later scholarship simply summarizes them (P4, P5)—historians regard Cydron’s Bexil origin as firmly established with high confidence.

All of the surviving evidence points to a straightforward nautical origin. In early seafaring slang a “drimbol” simply meant a broken or useless compass; therefore “to catch a drimbol” was the misfortune of ending up with (or being guided by) such a compass, i.e. finding oneself helplessly off-course.

Supporting evidence
• 1598 Charter of the Worshipful Company of Instrument Makers (P2): fines any merchant who sells “a drimbol”, explicitly glossed as a broken compass – the earliest known written definition.
• c. 1650 engraved binnacle housing, Artifact 890-B (P3), reading “Here lies our drimbol”, independently corroborates the object-meaning in a physical, datable artefact.
• 1745 Captain Elias Thorne’s Naval Glossary (P1) gives the first dictionary-style entry: “a drimbol: a broken compass; to catch a drimbol – to be hopelessly lost at sea”.

Secondary syntheses in modern scholarship (P4, P5) merely summarise those primary sources.

How well established?  Multiple independent primary sources—legal, material, and lexicographical—span nearly 150 years and all give the same sense.  No competing etymology is attested.  Accordingly, the origin is regarded as secure and well established by historical-linguistic standards.

All primary data sources we have agree on exactly the same figure: 14.2 % of the labour force in the Kholtar mining district is unemployed.

Evidence behind the 14.2 % figure
1. Kholtar Labor Registry (P1) – an administrative census of everyone who files taxes or unemployment claims: 14,200 registered job-seekers out of 100,000 working-age residents → 14.2 %.
2. Statistical Survey Institute household survey (P2) – 5,000 randomly sampled households interviewed with standard ILO methodology: point estimate 14.2 %.
3. Kholtar Amalgamated Miners Union membership records (P3) – proportion of members claiming out-of-work benefits yields 14.2 %.

How reliable is it?
• Convergence: Three independent primary sources (administrative register, large-scale random survey, union ledger) all converge on the same number, increasing credibility.
• Data quality: 
  – Administrative registry (P1) is usually considered high-quality for formal employment but can under-count informal workers. 
  – Survey (P2) has a large enough sample (≈5 % of households) to keep sampling error around ±1 percentage point and follows accepted ILO definitions. 
  – Union data (P3) is narrower in scope but provides an internal consistency check for miners themselves.
• Overall assessment: evidence is strong and mutually reinforcing, though—like any labour-market statistic—it may miss informal or unregistered workers and carries normal survey sampling error. Taking these caveats into account, the 14.2 % estimate is well-supported and likely accurate to within roughly ±1 percentage point.

All available records credit Marnik Sol as the first person to run the subterranean rapids of the Xylari Depths. This claim is strongly documented: (1) an official certification in the Global Speleological Society log (primary source P1), (2) contemporaneous telemetry and GPS data confirming the traverse (primary source P3, echoed in P5), and (3) an eyewitness expedition diary entry (primary source P2). Secondary summaries (P4, P5) repeat these primary records with no conflicting evidence. Overall, the achievement is considered well-established and highly reliable based on multiple independent primary documents.

The proverb is credited to the 19th-century writer Tymon Gress.  Support for this attribution is strong: (1) an 1892 signed manuscript of his poem The Alchemist’s Lament contains the exact line (P1); (2) a contemporaneous 1891 diary entry records him using the phrase in a public speech (P2); and (3) the Official Guild of Playwrights and Poets formally registered the aphorism to him in 1893 (P3).  Later reference works (P4, P5) repeat these primary sources.  Because multiple independent, contemporaneous documents tie the saying to Gress and no rival claimants appear in the record, the attribution is considered very well established.

The depth of the Sunken Caldera of Mynor is 1,845 meters. This figure is strongly supported: it comes from a 2018 multibeam-echosounder survey (P1), is adopted as the official value in the Ministry of Topography’s geographic database (P2) and derivative references (P4, P5), and is independently confirmed by a direct submersible measurement recorded in the Nereus dive log (P3). Because the same value is reported by two primary data sets that used different methods (instrumented survey and in-situ depth gauge) and is accepted by governmental and scientific publications, the measurement is considered highly reliable, with only normal instrumental uncertainty (on the order of a few metres) remaining.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the azure-tufted Plennet is 86 years. This figure is supported by three independent primary observations—a continuously monitored captive bird (Global Avian Registry ID 449-ATP), a wild bird dated by sclerochronology (ATP-W-01), and a banded free-living individual followed from 1912-1998—plus secondary reviews that cite these data. Because multiple, well-documented records converge on the same age and are accepted by authoritative sources, the 86-year value is strongly supported as the species’ verified maximum; however, it still rests on only a few individuals, so the absolute biological limit could be higher.

The spring-loaded Droxian seed-drill was invented in 1683.  

Reliability of the date: very high. Three independent primary sources converge on 1683: (1) the original Royal Patent Office record dated 4 May 1683 (P1); (2) dendrochronological and metallurgical analysis of the surviving prototype, which scientifically dates its construction to 1683 (P3); and (3) a contemporary farmer’s diary entry from the same year noting the new device (P2). Secondary narratives (P4, P5) simply repeat these primary findings. Because the evidence includes both documentary records and modern scientific dating of the physical artifact, historians regard the 1683 date as firmly established, with only minimal room for doubt.
